scenes.heading: Volume of pyramids and cones
scenes.sub: Why a cone holds exactly one-third
scenes.say: How much sand is in a pile, or how much water fits in a paper cone? Today you’ll find the volume of pyramids and cones.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Three cone cups of water exactly fill a matching cylinder cup
scenes.science: A cone holds ⅓ of the cylinder with the same base and height
scenes.breaks: Real paper bends and water spills, so it is only roughly three. The ⅓ rule is exact.
scenes.say: Imagine a cylinder cup and a cone cup with the same top and the same height. Fill the cone and tip it into the cylinder. It takes exactly three cones to fill the cylinder, so the cone holds one third as much.

scenes.heading: The one-third rule
scenes.say: For any pyramid, the volume is one third times the area of the base times the perpendicular height. For a cone, the base is a circle, so it is one third pi r squared h.

scenes.heading: A square pyramid
scenes.say: Here is a square pyramid with base edges of nine centimetres, then its perpendicular height of ten centimetres. The base area is eighty-one. One third of eighty-one times ten is two hundred and seventy cubic centimetres.
scenes.caption: A square pyramid with base edges 9 cm and height 10 cm. A = 81 cm². V = ⅓ × 81 × 10 = 270 cm³.

scenes.heading: Slant height? Find h first
scenes.say: This cone has radius six and slant height ten. The formula needs the perpendicular height, so use Pythagoras first: ten squared minus six squared is sixty-four, so h is eight. Then one third times pi times thirty-six times eight is ninety-six pi, about three hundred and one point six cubic centimetres.
scenes.caption: r = 6, slant 10. h² = 100 − 36 = 64, so h = 8. V = ⅓ × π × 36 × 8 = 96π ≈ 301.6 cm³.

scenes.heading: Working backwards
scenes.question: A cone has volume 100π cm³ and radius 5 cm. Find its height.
scenes.say: A cone has volume one hundred pi and radius five. Substitute: one third times pi times twenty-five times h equals one hundred pi. Divide by pi and multiply by three: twenty-five h equals three hundred. So h is twelve centimetres.
scenes.caption: Volume 100π, radius 5. ⅓ × π × 25 × h = 100π. Divide by π, multiply by 3: 25h = 300. h = 12 cm.

scenes.say: Recap. Pyramid volume is one third times base area times height. Cone volume is one third pi r squared h. Always use the perpendicular height. For composite solids, add or subtract the parts. Now try the practice questions!
